blocks.title: You'll want to know: さんぱい

segments.text: さんぱい — sanpai — "a visit to worship (at a shrine or temple)".
かぞくで てらに さんぱいに いきました。 — kazoku de tera ni sanpai ni ikimashita — "My family went to the temple to worship."

さんぱい (sanpai) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are san, "visit" (Middle Chinese tshom) and hai, "worship" (peajH), joined as sanpai (KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese in Baxter's transcription).
One more word for getting around.

てらで ふるい ぶつぞうを みました。 — tera de furui butsuzō o mimashita — "I saw an old statue at the temple."

ぶつぞう (butsuzō) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are butsu, "Buddha" (Middle Chinese bjut) and zō, "statue" (zjangX) (KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese in Baxter's transcription).

この てらの だいぶつは たかいです。 — kono tera no daibutsu wa takai desu — "The great statue at this temple is tall."

だいぶつ (daibutsu) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are dai, "large" (Middle Chinese dajH) and butsu, "Buddha" (bjut) (KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese in Baxter's transcription).

ほんどうで くつを ぬぎました。 — hondō de kutsu o nugimashita — "We took off our shoes in the main hall."

ほんどう (hondō) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are hon, "main" (Middle Chinese pwonX) and dō, "hall" (dang) (KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese in Baxter's transcription).

segments.text: Before the new one: say the Japanese for a great statue of the Buddha, then the Japanese for the main hall of a temple.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: おがむ

segments.text: おがむ — ogamu — "to pray with joined hands".
ほんどうの まえで おがみました。 — hondō no mae de ogamimashita — "I put my hands together in front of the main hall."
Polite おがみます, ogamimasu; a godan verb. Past (polite): そぼが ほんどうで おがみました。, sobo ga hondō de ogamimashita.
おがむ (ogamu) is a native Japanese word (wago), inherited rather than borrowed from Chinese; its kanji was attached later as a kun'yomi (JMdict).
One more word for getting around.
